The sequence “in those days, after that tribulation” (13:24) puts the coming after the tribulation, which fits a posttribulational rapture. The disciples are addressed as representatives of the church in the gospel's mission to all nations (13:10).

Pretribulational dispensationalists argue that the elect here are tribulation saints (often Jewish), not the raptured church. Preterists argue that “prophetic telescoping” does not answer the explicit time limit in 13:30.

Mark 13:14-27 describes the future tribulation and the abomination set up by the Antichrist in a rebuilt temple, followed by Christ's visible coming. The “elect” are believers on earth during that period, especially the Jewish remnant. “This generation” means the one that sees these final signs.

Jesus calls the tribulation unique in all history (13:19), and the coming involves cosmic upheaval and a universal gathering (13:27). Dispensationalists argue that these exceed anything that occurred in AD 70.

Critics answer that hyperbolic “never before” language is used of other local judgments in the Old Testament (Ezekiel 5:9; Daniel 9:12), and that Mark gives no sign of a two-thousand-year gap or a rebuilt temple.

Every element of Mark 13, including the coming of the Son of Man and the gathering of the elect, was fulfilled by AD 70. Since the question in 13:4 asks only about “these things”, the whole answer refers to them, and 13:30 sets its limit.

Full preterists treat Mark's wording as their strongest Olivet evidence, because there is no separate question about the end of the world, and they argue that the “day or hour” of 13:32 is the hour of the same event.

Critics answer that other New Testament texts link the coming to a bodily resurrection and a renewed creation (Romans 8:18-23; 1 Corinthians 15), neither of which occurred in AD 70. They also note that this position lies outside the historic creeds.
The Olivet Discourse (Luke)

Luke's account replaces the “abomination of desolation” with the plain warning “when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies” (21:20). Jerusalem will be trampled by Gentiles “until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled” (21:24). Then come signs in sun, moon and stars and the Son of Man coming in a cloud. Believers are to lift up their heads, because their redemption is drawing near (21:28); this generation will not pass away until all has taken place (21:32).

Luke explicitly ties the abomination to the Roman siege of AD 70, which preterists take as the key to the parallels. But he also adds “the times of the Gentiles” (21:24), which seems to place an open-ended period between the city's fall and the coming of the Son of Man. Everything turns on how 21:24 relates to 21:25-28.

Luke is the inspired interpreter of the parallels: the desolation is the Roman siege, and the “days of vengeance” (21:22) are the fulfilment of the curses on covenant-breaking Jerusalem. Some partial preterists also read the cosmic signs and the coming in 21:25-28 as the AD 70 judgment-vindication, with “redemption” referring to the church's deliverance from its persecutors; others take 21:24 as a hinge and 21:25-36 as future.

Luke's language is concrete and local (armies, Judea, those in the country, 21:20-21). The phrase “all that is written” being fulfilled (21:22) presents AD 70 as the climax of covenant judgment. The time text in 21:32 matches Matthew and Mark.

Futurists argue that the “times of the Gentiles” in 21:24 opens an indefinite period after AD 70, and that the coming of 21:27 comes after it, so 21:25-28 must be later than AD 70. Partial preterists are themselves divided on this point.

With most partial preterists, postmillennialists see 21:20-24 as fulfilled in AD 70 and the “times of the Gentiles” as the long era of the gospel among the nations. Many (following the Puritans and Romans 11:25) expect that this era will eventually be followed by a large turning of the Jews to Christ, which will bring further blessing to the world.

“Until” (achri) in 21:24 implies that Jerusalem's trampling has a limit, which parallels Paul's “until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in” (Romans 11:25). That supports the hope of a future ingathering of Israel within history.
Critics argue that the Romans 11 link is not clearly made by Luke and that 21:24 may simply refer to Gentile domination until the end, not to a period of growing gospel success.

Luke separates the two horizons more clearly than Matthew or Mark. 21:8-24 concerns AD 70; 21:24 opens the church age (the times of the Gentiles); 21:25-28 describes the Second Coming at its end. The discourse thus supports a single future return after an indefinite period, with no separate millennial era.

The structure of the chapter is a near event (the siege), then an open-ended period, then the final coming, which matches the amillennial picture of the present age. The universal language of 21:35 (“all who dwell on the face of the whole earth”) points beyond Judea.

Preterists ask how 21:32 (“all has taken place”) can include an event thousands of years later; amillennial answers usually take “all” to refer to the signs leading up to the end, which preterists find strained.

Luke shows the pattern that historic premillennialists find throughout the discourse: Jerusalem's fall, a long Gentile age, then the posttribulational return of Christ, at which believers' redemption, meaning bodily resurrection and the gathering of the church, arrives (21:28). Many also read 21:24 as implying a future restoration of Israel.

The redemption of 21:28 parallels Romans 8:23 (the redemption of our bodies), suggesting the resurrection at the end. The open-ended times of the Gentiles makes room for a future coming after a long period.
Preterists press 21:32 again; dispensationalists argue that Luke's focus on Jerusalem points to a specifically Jewish future programme, which historic premillennialism does not develop.

Dispensationalists usually concede that Luke 21:20-24 describes AD 70, unlike Matthew 24:15. They argue that Luke records a different part of Jesus' teaching, while 21:25-28 jumps forward to the end of the future tribulation and Christ's return. The “times of the Gentiles”, which began with Nebuchadnezzar and continue today, end when Christ restores Jerusalem and Israel.

The “until” of 21:24 implies that Jerusalem will one day no longer be trampled, which fits national Israel's restoration. The different wording in Luke (armies rather than an abomination in the holy place) allows Matthew's abomination to remain a separate, future event.

Critics say that treating Luke 21:20 as a different event from the parallel Matthew 24:15 and Mark 13:14, which sit in the same place in the discourse with the same command to flee, is special pleading driven by the system.

The whole chapter, including the coming in a cloud and the believers' redemption, was fulfilled within the generation (21:32). The times of the Gentiles are the short period of Roman trampling in AD 66-70, which ended with the consummation of the kingdom (21:31).
Full preterists point to the time limit in 21:32 and the near-redemption language of 21:28, which is addressed to the disciples (“your redemption”).

Critics argue that the Gentile trampling of Jerusalem continued for centuries after AD 70, and that “redemption” elsewhere includes the bodily resurrection (Romans 8:23), which full preterism does not expect in a physical sense. They note that this view lies outside creedal orthodoxy.
The Statue and the Stone

Nebuchadnezzar's dream shows a statue of gold, silver, bronze, iron and iron mixed with clay, representing successive kingdoms. A stone cut out “without hands” strikes the statue's feet, destroys it entirely and grows into a great mountain that fills the earth. Daniel explains that “in the days of those kings” God will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed (2:44).

When the stone strikes, and how the kingdom grows. If the stone is Christ's first advent in the days of Rome and the kingdom then grows gradually to fill the earth, the passage supports a present, expanding kingdom. If the stone strikes a future, revived form of the fourth kingdom suddenly at the Second Coming, it supports premillennialism. Conservative interpreters usually identify the kingdoms as Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece and Rome; critical scholars usually make them Babylon, Media, Persia and Greece.

The stone is Christ and his kingdom, set up during the Roman empire at his first coming. Growing from a small stone into a mountain that fills the earth is a picture of the gradual, worldwide spread of his kingdom in history through the gospel, until it overwhelms all rival powers. Daniel 2 is thus one of postmillennialism's key Old Testament proofs of the kingdom's growth before the end.

The kingdom is established “in the days of those kings” (2:44), meaning during the fourth empire, which fits Christ's announcement that the kingdom had come near (Mark 1:15). The growth image matches the parables of the mustard seed and leaven (Matthew 13:31-33).

Premillennialists answer that in the dream the stone first destroys the statue completely, so the destruction is sudden and comes before the growth, which does not fit gradual conversion. Amillennialists agree that the kingdom came at the first advent but doubt that the mountain describes a stage of history before the return.

The stone is Christ's kingdom, inaugurated at his first advent during the Roman era. It is spiritual and heavenly in origin (“cut without hands”), already present, and will be consummated when Christ returns to destroy all opposing kingdoms. The mountain that fills the earth is the final, universal kingdom, partly realised now in the church among all nations and fully realised in the new creation.

Jesus may allude to the stone in Luke 20:18, linking it to his own person. The kingdom “shall stand forever” (2:44), which suits a kingdom that runs straight from the first advent into eternity rather than a temporary millennium.

Postmillennialists say amillennialism does not take seriously the growth of the stone into a mountain within history. Premillennialists say it reads the crushing of the kingdoms as gradual or spiritual when the text describes a decisive blow.

The kingdom of God was inaugurated by Christ, but the decisive smashing of world empires described by the stone comes at his return, which brings in the earthly kingdom. Ladd stresses the “already and not yet”: the kingdom's power is present now, but its visible triumph over the kingdoms of the world is still ahead.
The stone does not coexist with the statue; it destroys it at one blow (2:34-35), which fits a cataclysmic return (compare Revelation 11:15; 19:15).
Critics note that the stone appears “in the days of those kings” (the fourth kingdom), which seems to fix its arrival in Roman times rather than in the distant future.

The feet and ten toes represent a final, future phase of the Roman empire, a ten-king confederacy that has not yet existed. Christ, the stone, will strike it suddenly at his Second Coming, destroy Gentile world power and set up the millennial kingdom on earth, with Jerusalem as its centre. The kingdom does not grow gradually within the present age.

The toes and the ten horns of Daniel 7:24 and Revelation 17:12 correspond, and no historical confederacy of ten kings fits them. The striking is catastrophic, not gradual, which matches the description of the return in Revelation 19.

Critics say Daniel gives no hint of a gap between the legs and the feet of the fourth kingdom, and the text dates the stone to the days of those kings. A revived Rome is read into the passage rather than drawn from it.

The four kingdoms are Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece and Rome; the mixed iron and clay are the divided kingdoms of Western Europe after Rome's fall, which have never been successfully joined by marriage alliances or conquest. Christ's kingdom, begun at his first coming, will finally replace them.
Historicists (Newton, Barnes) point to the long-term failure of every attempt to reunite Europe (Charlemagne, Napoleon) as striking evidence that the prophecy is being fulfilled in history.
Critics argue that the European focus is a narrow reading of a prophecy about God's universal kingdom, and that historical identifications are elastic enough to fit almost any outcome.

The stone struck the fourth (Roman) kingdom in the first century: Christ came during the Roman empire, and his kingdom was established at his ascension and vindicated in the judgment of AD 70. Since then it grows into the mountain that fills the earth, as the Christian faith outlasts and replaces the old Roman order.
The fourth empire is Rome, so the stone's coming has to be placed in the Roman era. Rome's own conversion and eventual collapse while the church continued are taken to illustrate the vision.
Futurists reply that Rome continued for centuries after the first advent and that the statue was not destroyed “all together” (2:35) in the first century.
The Four Beasts and the Son of Man

Daniel sees four beasts rise from the sea. The fourth has ten horns, and a little horn among them speaks boastfully and wages war on the saints for “a time, times and half a time” (7:25). The Ancient of Days sits in judgment, and “one like a son of man” comes with the clouds of heaven to the Ancient of Days and receives everlasting dominion (7:13-14). The kingdom is then given to the saints of the Most High (7:18, 22, 27).

Who the little horn is (Antiochus IV, a Roman emperor, the papacy, or a future Antichrist) and what direction the Son of Man's “coming” takes. In 7:13 he comes to the Ancient of Days, which many read as Christ's ascension and enthronement; futurists read it as his return to earth. Jesus' use of the verse (Mark 14:62) is central.

The Son of Man ascends to the Ancient of Days (7:13), which is Christ's ascension and enthronement, and receives a kingdom in which all peoples, nations and languages will serve him (7:14). That service is achieved through the gospel in history. The saints share his rule (7:18, 27), which postmillennialists connect with the church's task of discipling the nations.

The direction is explicit: the figure comes to the Ancient of Days, not down to earth. Jesus' post-resurrection claim to all authority (Matthew 28:18) echoes 7:14 in the Greek translation. The worldwide scope (all nations serving) shapes the postmillennial hope.

Critics note that the saints receive the kingdom only after the little horn's persecution and the judgment (7:21-22, 26-27), which places the full kingdom at the end, not in a gradual process within history.

7:13-14 is fulfilled in Christ's ascension and heavenly enthronement, and the saints receive the kingdom now in principle and at the end in fullness. The little horn is a type of the final Antichrist: an anti-God ruler who persecutes the church. Antiochus IV (pictured in Daniel 8) is an early instance, and a final figure will appear before the end. The “time, times and half a time” is symbolic of the limited period of the church's suffering, picked up in Revelation 12-13.

The book of Revelation reuses Daniel 7 for the church age (the beast of Revelation 13 combines Daniel's four beasts), which suggests the pattern is ongoing. Jesus' words to the high priest (Mark 14:62) say the Sanhedrin will see him enthroned, which fits ascension.

Dispensationalists argue that the little horn's specific actions and final destruction at the judgment (7:11, 26) describe one individual at the end, not a recurring type. Preterists argue that the ruler should be found in the first century.

The fourth beast is Rome and its later forms; the little horn is the future Antichrist, who persecutes the saints (the church) during the final tribulation. The Son of Man's receiving of the kingdom is enthronement, but its outworking on earth, when the saints take the kingdom (7:22), comes at Christ's return, followed by his earthly reign.

The saints are persecuted by the horn until the judgment (7:21-22), which suggests that the church goes through the final tribulation, a key posttribulational point. Jesus in Matthew 24:30 uses Daniel 7:13 language for a future coming.
Amillennialists say that Daniel's kingdom is eternal (7:14, 27), with no intermediate millennial stage. Preterists say that Jesus applied Daniel 7:13 to events within that generation.

The ten horns are a future ten-nation confederacy arising from a revived Roman empire. The little horn is the coming Antichrist, who will rule it and persecute Israel and tribulation saints for three and a half years (the second half of Daniel's seventieth week). The Son of Man then comes in glory to destroy him and establish the millennial kingdom, in which the saints reign.

Daniel 7, Daniel 9:27, 2 Thessalonians 2:3-8 and Revelation 13 describe a single blasphemous persecutor who rules for the same period (three and a half years, 42 months, 1260 days), which suggests one future person.

Critics argue that the dispensational scheme requires an unmentioned gap of millennia within the fourth beast. Many also reject reading the “coming” of 7:13 as a descent when the text describes an ascent to God's throne.

The little horn is the papacy, rising among the ten kingdoms that succeeded Rome, uprooting three of them (in one common Protestant reckoning the Heruli, Vandals and Ostrogoths; Newton proposed a different three), speaking great words and persecuting the saints. By the year-day principle, its “time, times and half a time” is 1,260 years, often dated from AD 538 to 1798, when Napoleon's general took the pope prisoner. This was the dominant Protestant view from the Reformation into the nineteenth century.

Historicists point to the long reign of papal power, its claims to change “times and law” (7:25), and the striking end of its political power in 1798. They note that the Reformers, the Westminster divines and Newton held this reading.

Critics argue that different historicists have assigned different start and end dates, and that the year-day principle is not a stated rule of prophecy. Roman Catholic and many Protestant scholars also reject the identification as polemical.

The fourth beast is Rome; the little horn is a first-century persecuting ruler (proposals vary, including Nero or the Flavian emperors). The Son of Man came to the Ancient of Days in the ascension, and his kingdom was publicly vindicated in AD 70, when the saints “possessed the kingdom” (7:22) as the old covenant order ended.
Jesus applies Daniel 7:13 to what the Sanhedrin would see (Mark 14:62) and to the coming within his generation (Matthew 24:30, 34). Placing the vision in the Roman era fits the four-empire sequence.

Critics argue that no single first-century emperor clearly matches all the horn's details, and that proposals vary widely among preterists. Others argue that Daniel 7 should be read alongside chapters 8 and 11, which point to Antiochus.

Daniel 7 was entirely fulfilled by AD 70: the Son of Man received his kingdom, the persecuting powers were judged, and the saints took possession of the everlasting kingdom when the old covenant ended. Nothing in the vision remains to be fulfilled.
Full preterists link 7:22 (the time came for the saints to possess the kingdom) with Jesus' promise that the kingdom would come in power within the lifetime of his hearers (Mark 9:1).

Critics point out that Daniel 7 describes the destruction of all opposing kingdoms and the universal service of all peoples, which did not occur in AD 70. They note that the view rejects the creedal hope of a future return.
The Seventy Weeks

Gabriel tells Daniel that seventy “sevens” (shavuʿim) are decreed for his people and city: to finish transgression, put an end to sin, atone for iniquity, bring in everlasting righteousness, seal vision and prophet, and anoint a most holy place (or one). From a decree to rebuild Jerusalem to an anointed one are seven sevens and sixty-two sevens; after the sixty-two, an anointed one is “cut off”, and the people of a coming prince destroy the city and sanctuary. “He” confirms a covenant with many for one seven, and in its middle puts an end to sacrifice.

Whether the seventy weeks run continuously, with the seventieth fulfilled in Christ's ministry and death (most preterist, postmillennial, amillennial and historicist readings), or whether there is a gap after the sixty-ninth, with the seventieth a future seven-year tribulation (dispensational). The crux is the antecedent of “he” in 9:27 (Messiah, or the coming prince) and which decree starts the count (538, 458 or 445/444 BC).

The seventy weeks run continuously. Counting from Artaxerxes' decree to Ezra (458/457 BC), 483 years reach AD 26/27 and Jesus' baptism. In the middle of the seventieth week the Messiah is cut off, and his once-for-all sacrifice ends the validity of temple sacrifices. He “confirms the covenant with many” (the new covenant, compare Matthew 26:28). The destruction of AD 70 is the consequence of his rejection. The six goals of 9:24 are accomplished by Christ's atoning work.

The six goals of 9:24 are redemptive (atonement, everlasting righteousness) and fit the cross. Nothing in the text signals an interruption of the count. The most natural antecedent of “he” is the Messiah, the main subject of the prophecy, and “confirming a covenant with many” echoes Isaiah 53:11-12.

Dispensationalists argue that the nearest antecedent of “he” is “the prince who is to come” (9:26), and that the destruction of the city in 9:26 falls after the sixty-nine weeks but is not placed in the seventieth, implying a gap. They also note that the 458 BC decree is about the temple and worship rather than rebuilding the city.

Most Reformed amillennialists also see the prophecy fulfilled in Christ. E. J. Young took the weeks as symbolic periods culminating in Christ; Meredith Kline argued that the Messiah confirms the covenant and that the seventieth week extends symbolically through the church age, so the second half corresponds to the church's tribulation (the 1,260 days of Revelation 11-12). Riddlebarger is broadly sympathetic to Kline's reading.

Revelation reuses the half-week period (“time, times and half a time”, 42 months) for the church's experience between the advents, which suggests that the second half of the seventieth week is symbolically extended. The messianic reading of 9:27 has a long history in the church.

Dispensationalists argue that a symbolic stretching of the seventieth week is itself a kind of gap. Postmillennial preterists argue that the plain arithmetic fits Christ's ministry without extending the week.

Historic premillennialists are divided. Many accept the messianic reading of 9:25-26 (Christ's coming and death) while leaving open a final fulfilment of 9:27's desolator in the end-time Antichrist, as Jesus' use of the abomination in Matthew 24:15 and Paul's man of lawlessness (2 Thessalonians 2:4) may suggest. Others adopt a futurist seventieth week without the full dispensational framework.

Jesus treats the abomination of desolation as still future in his day (Matthew 24:15), which seems to place at least part of Daniel 9:27 after the crucifixion. Early church writers such as Irenaeus and Hippolytus already saw a future Antichrist in the last week.

Preterists answer that Jesus' “abomination” was fulfilled within his generation in AD 70, and dispensationalists answer that the divided historic premillennial approach lacks a coherent account of the gap.

Sixty-nine weeks (483 years of 360 days each) run from Artaxerxes' decree to Nehemiah (444 BC) to Christ's triumphal entry (Hoehner: AD 33). Messiah is cut off after the sixty-ninth week; then the prophetic clock stops for the church age. The seventieth week is a future seven-year tribulation that begins when the coming prince (the Antichrist, from the people who destroyed the temple, the Romans) makes a covenant with Israel; he breaks it in the middle by stopping temple sacrifices.

The events of 9:26 (the cutting off and the destruction of the city) come “after” the sixty-two weeks, not in the seventieth, which, Ice argues, implies a gap. The six goals of 9:24 include Israel's national restoration, which has not happened. Jesus placed the abomination in the future (Matthew 24:15).

Critics say a 2,000-year gap within a counted period of seventy weeks would make the counting meaningless, and that the antecedent of “he” in 9:27 is more naturally the Messiah, since “the prince” in 9:26 is subordinate to “the people”. Hoehner's 360-day year calculation is also disputed.

The seventy weeks were completely fulfilled in the first century. Christ's work accomplished the goals of 9:24; he was cut off in the middle of the seventieth week; and the desolation of 9:26-27 is the Roman destruction of Jerusalem, which Jesus explicitly linked to Daniel (Matthew 24:15). Some (Gentry) end the seventieth week around AD 34 with the gospel turning to the Gentiles; AD 70 is the outworking of the covenant judgment.
Jesus' warning about the abomination (Matthew 24:15) and Luke's parallel (Luke 21:20) tie Daniel's desolation to the Roman siege. A continuous count fits the arithmetic and the theological goals.

Critics observe that AD 70 falls nearly forty years after the end of the seventieth week on this reading, so 9:26-27 must refer to events outside the seventy weeks, which they see as a gap of another kind.

The seventieth week extends to AD 70 and includes the consummation of all prophecy. The goals of 9:24 (to seal vision and prophecy, bring in everlasting righteousness) were completed at the destruction of the temple, so all prophecy, including the resurrection, was fulfilled then.
Full preterists argue that “sealing up vision and prophet” means the fulfilment of all prophecy, which places every remaining expectation, including the resurrection, within the seventy weeks.

Critics argue that this stretches the seventieth week to about forty years, which is no more natural than the dispensational gap, and that the claim that all prophecy has been fulfilled conflicts with the creedal confession of a future return and resurrection.

Classical historicists (Newton, Barnes, Elliott) read the seventy weeks as fulfilled in Christ: counting from Artaxerxes' seventh year (457 BC), 483 years reach AD 27 and the Messiah's public ministry. They regarded this prophecy as the clearest confirmation of the year-day principle, since its “weeks” must be weeks of years.
The accuracy of the count in years, starting from a known decree and ending in Christ's ministry, is offered as a template for interpreting other prophetic periods in years.

Critics accept that the seventy weeks are “sevens” of years but deny that this justifies applying a day-for-a-year rule to the other numbers in Daniel and Revelation, where the text speaks of days and months.
The Man of Lawlessness

Concerning the coming (parousia) of Christ and our gathering to him, Paul tells the Thessalonians not to be shaken by claims that the Day of the Lord has already come. It will not come unless the apostasia (rebellion or apostasy) comes first and the man of lawlessness is revealed, who sets himself up in the temple of God. Something (neuter, to katechon, 2:6) and someone (masculine, ho katechōn, 2:7) restrains him now; the mystery of lawlessness is “already at work”. When the restrainer is removed, the lawless one will be revealed, and the Lord Jesus will destroy him with the breath of his mouth and the appearance of his coming.

Who the restrainer is, what the apostasia is, and whether the man of lawlessness is a first-century figure (Nero, or a Jewish leader in the AD 70 crisis), the papacy, or a future Antichrist. Also contested is which coming is in view: the parousia that destroys him (2:8) could be the final return or, on preterist readings, the AD 70 judgment.

Gentry reads 2 Thessalonians 2 as concerned with first-century events. The man of lawlessness is Nero; the restrainer is Claudius and Roman law (noting the claudere, “to shut up”, wordplay), which held Nero back until his accession in AD 54. The temple is the Jerusalem temple; the apostasy is the Jewish revolt against Rome and against Christ. The “coming” is Christ's judgment-coming in AD 70. Warfield (1886) similarly read the man of sin as the line of Roman emperors.

Paul's readers knew who the restrainer was (2:5-6) and the mystery was “already at work” (2:7), which suggests a first-century referent. A standing Jerusalem temple existed when Paul wrote, and Nero's self-deifying claims and his persecution are well documented.

Critics argue that Nero never set himself up in the Jerusalem temple, and that the one who is destroyed by Christ's coming (2:8) is linked to the parousia of 2:1, which includes the believers' “gathering” to Christ, a final, future event. Many partial preterists themselves hold the passage is about the end.

Before Christ returns there will be a great apostasy within the visible church, and a final Antichrist will appear. The spirit of lawlessness is at work in every age (2:7; 1 John 2:18), and it culminates in a person. The “temple of God” may be the church (Paul's normal use of naos in 1 Corinthians 3:16 and 2 Corinthians 6:16) where false religion takes over. Amillennialists vary on the restrainer: the preaching of the gospel, God's providential order, or civil government.

Paul joins the parousia with the believers' gathering (2:1) and with the destruction of the lawless one (2:8), so all three happen at the one return. Paul speaks of the mystery already working, which fits a recurring pattern with a final climax.
Preterists argue that Paul's readers would have understood the temple as the actual Jerusalem temple, and dispensationalists argue that a spiritualised temple weakens the force of the passage.

Many postmillennialists (Gentry, and Warfield before him) take the partial-preterist view, so the passage does not predict an apostasy at the end of the church age and does not undercut a hopeful view of history. Others, including older postmillennialists, place the apostasy and man of sin later in history (the papacy, for many Puritans) or allow for the final rebellion of Revelation 20:7-9 before the return.
